Analysis of the target, in-distribution uncertainty, out-of-distribution uncertainty, and training residual distributions suggest that future work focus on understanding empirical uncertainties in the feature input space for cases where ensemble prediction variances do not accurately capture the missing information required for the model to generalize.

title: Exciton diffusion dynamics with dissipation in organic molecular semiconductors
abstract: Exciton diffusion governs energy transport in organic molecular crystals and limits the performance of optoelectronic devices. Accurate simulation requires capturing correlated electron-nuclear motion, yet existing approaches rely on empirical treatments. Here we derive a representation-free dissipation correction for exciton dynamics from the exact factorization formalism, in which a dimensionless factor ξ quantifies dissipation through the ratio of quantum and classical nuclear momentum. Within a classical path framework, ξ is obtained from site energy fluctuations in molecular dynamics non-empirically. The exciton Hamiltonian is constructed using a semiempirical approach to describe local excitations and excitonic couplings in large systems. Applications to anthracene, perylenetetracarboxylic diimide, and quinoid merocyanine reproduce distinct exciton transport regimes ranging from localized hopping to more delocalized transport, demonstrating that an account for dissipation is essential for realistic exciton dynamics.

title: Lattice free energies of molecular crystals using normalizing flow
abstract: Accurate free-energy calculations are essential for predicting thermodynamic stability in complex molecular materials, such as the polymorphic crystal landscapes of pharmaceutical molecules. Classical methods such as the Einstein crystal method (ECM) provide benchmark accuracy but are computationally prohibitive in larger crystal landscapes generated by Crystal Structure Prediction. Here, we develop a scalable framework for the anharmonic free-energy ranking of molecular crystals, based on targeted free-energy perturbation. In particular, we utilise the targeted Bennett acceptance ratio (tBAR) method, where the targeting step employs a bijective map learned via a normalising flow. The maps are trained to analytically transform supercell configurations between the crystal Boltzmann ensembles of interest and an analytical reference state. Exact likelihoods, in turn, enable reliable lattice free-energy estimates directly from physical molecular dynamics data, without alchemical sampling. The method handles supercells with up to 3 × 10 3 degrees of freedom and permits multi-state training with a single model. Validation across succinic acid, Veliparib, and Mivebresib demonstrates excellent agreement with ECM at significantly lower cost. By combining statistical mechanics and machine-learning expressivity, this approach advances anharmonic free energies towards automation and high-throughput applications in molecular and materials design.

title: Reaching the thermodynamic limit of periodic CCSD cohesive energies and band gaps
abstract: The high computational cost of periodic coupled-cluster theory has limited the density of Brillouin zone sampling, yielding finite-size errors that need to be removed by extrapolation. Here we report the development and application of a distributed-memory software implementation of periodic coupled-cluster theory with single and double excitations (CCSD) that runs efficiently on up to 12 nodes with 96 cores each. This new implementation allows ground-state and excited-state calculations in which the Brillouin zone is sampled with up to 6 3 = 216 k -points, allowing us to reliably extrapolate to the thermodynamic limit. For eight simple semiconductors and insulators, we report the cohesive energy and band gap, which are converged to 0.1 eV, providing definitive benchmark numbers for the CCSD level of theory. Compared to experimental values, average errors for the cohesive energy are 0.1–0.2 eV (typically an underestimate), and average errors for the band gap are about 0.4 eV (typically an overestimate).

title: The role of solid-melt interfaces in self-catalyzed growth kinetics of III-nitride semiconductors
abstract: Solid-melt interfaces govern metal-mediated epitaxy of gallium nitride (GaN) and related III-nitride semiconductors, yet a quantitative connection between interfacial structure and growth kinetics has remained elusive. Using atomistic simulations based on machine-learning interatomic potentials, we show that crystal orientation determines the local atomic arrangement and electrostatic character at the interface, inducing facet-dependent ordering in the adjacent melt. This ordering reshapes the N-transport free-energy landscape, substantially lowering migration barriers relative to pristine surfaces. Kinetic Monte Carlo simulations reveal that under realistic Ga-mediated molecular beam epitaxy (MBE) conditions, GaN grows in a diffusion-controlled, layer-by-layer regime, where the interface-normal adsorption free-energy landscape sets the dominant kinetic resistance. Combining facet-specific free-energy profiles with N diffusivity and solubility in liquid Ga, we develop a fitting-free model predicting growth rates of 0.01–0.04 nm/s, consistent with MBE-grown GaN nanoparticles. Similar ordering in other III-nitride systems indicates a generalizable route from atomistic energetics to anisotropic crystal growth kinetics.

title: Distortion states as robust embeddings for quantifying and forecasting atomistic damage from electron microscopy
abstract: We present an AI-driven framework that helps describe and predict damage at the atomistic level in irradiated materials. Rather than identifying discrete, visible defects, we define damage as a continuous spectrum of lattice distortions arising from atomic fluctuations. These distortions are encoded into a compact distortion state vector that unifies information from atomistic simulations and synthetic scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM). Deep-learning models learn to reconstruct this state directly from STEM images, linking experimental contrast to the underlying atomic disorder without annotations or expert intervention. Operating in this representation space, the framework can forecast the evolution of hidden defect populations from only a few dozen initial images. Thus, it opens new perspectives for understanding how atomic-scale fluctuations give rise to macroscopic degradation, laying the foundation for physics-based digital twins of materials.

title: Piezoelectric manipulation and stacking-dependent magnetism in ferrovalley materials
abstract: Coupling piezoelectricity to Berry-curvature-driven transport provides a route for mechanically controlling valley and layer degrees of freedom. Here, using first-principles calculations, we propose a piezoelectric polarization-mediated anomalous valley Hall effect (PAVHE) in 2 H - and 1 T -LaHF monolayers and extend this mechanism to a piezoelectric polarization-mediated layer Hall effect (PLHE) in stacked 2 H -LaHF bilayers. In the monolayers, spontaneous valley polarization, finite Berry curvature, and symmetry-allowed in-plane piezoelectricity enable strain-driven valley-selective Hall transport. A uniaxial strain of 0.1% produces estimated effective in-plane fields of 2.66 × 10 6 and 1.67 × 10 7 V/m in 2 H - and 1 T -LaHF, respectively. In the bilayer, spin-Hamiltonian and interlayer-hopping analyses reveal that the stacking-dependent balance between \({J}_{1\perp }\) and \({J}_{2\perp }\) governs the selection of the interlayer FM and AFM ground states. Combined with the layer character of the valley states, the in-plane piezoelectric response of the transport-active layer enables mechanically driven PLHE. These results provide a design principle for coupling piezoelectricity with valley- and layer-dependent Hall transport in two-dimensional magnetic materials.

title: Concerted mass transport governs anomalous diffusion in dynamically-stabilized bcc metals
abstract: Understanding the microscopic origin of anomalous self-diffusion near melting remains a central challenge in bcc metals. Here we combine ab initio and machine-learning interatomic-potential molecular dynamics (AIMD, MLIP-MD) to elucidate high-temperature mass transport in group-3–6 metals. Comparative AIMD simulations near melting at ambient pressure reveal a marked difference in mass-transport behavior between dynamically-stabilized group-3 and group-4 bcc metals and group-5 and group-6 metals; for which bcc is the intrinsically stable structure. In the former, characterized by strongly anharmonic energy landscapes, sufficiently large thermal displacements of individual atoms trigger cascades of cooperative transport, including ring exchanges and spontaneous formation and migration of vacancy–crowdion-like Frenkel pairs. In contrast, diffusion in group-5 and group-6 metals remains dominated by conventional vacancy mechanisms. Temperature-dependent MLIP-MD simulations of bcc Ti further show Arrhenius-like migration of isolated point defects upon cooling toward dynamical instability. Near melting, collective reactions in nominally pristine lattice regions provide an additional transport channel contributing to non-Arrhenius self-diffusion. Structural analysis reveals transient ω-like local environments as fingerprints of lattice softening accompanying these correlated dynamics. These results identify strong lattice anharmonicity as a key factor promoting collective transport in bcc metals and suggest a broader framework for high-temperature transport in crystalline solids.

title: OptiMat Alloys: a FAIR-aligned living database of multi-principal element alloys enabled by a conversational agent
abstract: Existing FAIR materials repositories can only serve pre-computed entries, so broad coverage is perpetually incomplete and cannot adapt to new questions on demand. We present OptiMat Alloys, a large language model-powered conversational agent for multi-principal element alloy exploration. Its central contribution is LLM-based workflow orchestration coupled to a living database : every calculation is performed on demand and persisted automatically with provenance in a local database, so asking a question produces provenance-rich, FAIR-aligned records without a separate deposition step. The agent is accessible through a web interface that requires no programming expertise ( low-barrier accessibility ) and reports uncertainty through cross-potential and cross-configuration validation ( built-in uncertainty quantification ). By coupling foundational machine learning interatomic potentials that cover nearly the entire periodic table with natural-language interaction, OptiMat Alloys enables targeted, on-demand computation guided by the user’s domain knowledge and brings computational alloy screening within reach of any materials scientist.

title: Physics-informed Bayesian optimization for quantitative high-resolution transmission electron microscopy
abstract: Quantitative high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) provides an indispensable means to understand structure-property relationships in atomic dimensions. Successful quantification requires reliable retrieval of essential atomic structural information despite artifacts arising from practically unavoidable imaging imperfections. Experimental observation combined with model-based iterative image simulation has enabled broad applications in quantitative structural and chemical determination of objects spanning zero to three dimensions. However, the large number of parameters involved makes the current multi-step, user-supervised iterative approach highly time-consuming, restricting its use to small sample areas and experienced users. In this work, we implement and apply a physics-informed Bayesian optimization (BO) framework to advance HRTEM quantification toward full automation and large-field-of-view analysis. Unlike conventional optimization methods, our approach adopts a stepwise strategy that fully leverages BO’s strength in handling high-dimensional parameter spaces, while its probabilistic engine efficiently refines the parameter space for rapid quantification. Using a BaTiO 3 single crystal that contains heavy, medium, and light elements as a model system, we demonstrate that the three-dimensional crystal structure can be determined from a single HRTEM image with a three- to four-order-of-magnitude improvement in time efficiency. This approach opens new avenues for fast, automated quantification over larger sample volumes and, promisingly, for in-situ applications.
